angle: a walk through a place that disappeared (the drive-in)
title: Saturday Night at the Drive-In, 1958. Here's What It Was Really Like

scenes.text: Sweetheart, you watch movies on a little phone, lying in bed. When I was a girl, we watched them in the car, under the stars, on a screen as big as a barn, with a thousand other families parked in rows around us. It was called the drive-in. And on a summer Saturday night in nineteen fifty-eight, there was no better place on earth. Let me take you there.
scenes.caption: THE DRIVE-IN

scenes.text: The first drive-in opened in Camden, New Jersey, in nineteen thirty-three. A man named Richard Hollingshead tested it in his own driveway, with a projector on the hood of his car and a sheet nailed between two trees. By the late fifties there were more than four thousand of them across America. Today there are only about three hundred left. Most of the ones I knew are shopping centers now.
scenes.caption: FOUR THOUSAND

scenes.text: Saturday drive-in night started right after supper. Mother made a grocery bag full of popcorn on the stove, with real butter and too much salt. She filled a thermos with Kool-Aid and wrapped a dozen baloney sandwiches in wax paper. You could buy food at the snack bar, but that was for rich people. We brought our own.
scenes.caption: A BAG OF POPCORN

scenes.text: Danny and I put our pajamas on before we left. Every kid did. Because the second movie went past midnight, and you'd fall asleep in the back seat, and your father would carry you into the house without waking you up. That's the best feeling in the world, sweetheart, being carried in from the car asleep. I hope somebody did it for you.
scenes.caption: PAJAMAS IN THE CAR

scenes.text: We piled into the Chevrolet, my father driving, Mother next to him, Danny and me in the back with pillows and a blanket and the dog. Yes, the dog came. Skipper loved the drive-in. And we drove out on Route thirty to the Springmill Drive-In, just outside of town, with the sun going down orange over the cornfields.
scenes.query: 1950s family car driving sunset country road
scenes.caption: OUT ON ROUTE THIRTY

scenes.text: At the gate there was a little booth with a man in a paper hat. A lot of drive-ins charged by the car, not by the person. A dollar a carload on Tuesday nights. On Saturdays it was fifty cents a person, and children under twelve got in free. So my father always said I was eleven. I was eleven for about three years.
scenes.caption: A DOLLAR A CARLOAD

scenes.text: And the teenagers, honey, oh, the teenagers. They'd come in a car with two boys in the front seat, and three more hiding in the trunk. Then they'd park in the back row and let them out. Everybody knew. The man in the paper hat knew. Sometimes he'd walk around the back of the car and knock on the trunk, just to scare them.
scenes.caption: THREE IN THE TRUNK

scenes.text: My father had his own drive-in rules, sweetheart. Park in the middle, not too close and not too far. Never next to a car full of teenagers. Never next to the snack bar, because of the noise. And always, always, back into the spot if it was a hot night, so you could open the trunk and sit on the tailgate. He'd been doing it since the war. He never once got it wrong.
scenes.caption: FATHER'S RULES

scenes.text: Inside, the field was rows and rows of little gravel hills, so your car tipped back and you could see the screen over the car in front of you. Every parking spot had a metal pole with a speaker hanging on it. You rolled your window down halfway, hooked the speaker over the glass, and turned the knob. The sound was terrible. Crackly and tinny. We loved it.
scenes.caption: THE SPEAKER

scenes.text: And people forgot to take the speaker off before they drove away. Every single night, sweetheart. You'd hear a crash of glass and a man swearing, and a car window would be lying in the gravel. The drive-ins lost thousands of speakers a year that way. My father did it once. Mother never let him forget it.
scenes.caption: CRASH

scenes.text: Before the movie there was a playground right under the screen, with swings and a merry-go-round and a little train. All the kids ran down there in their pajamas while it was still light. You'd swing as high as you could, and look up at that enormous white screen over your head, and wait for the sky to get dark enough.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYGROUND UNDER THE SCREEN

scenes.text: Then the lights went down, and the cartoons came on. Bugs Bunny, Tom and Jerry. And then the newsreel, with the world news. In nineteen fifty-eight it was all about the Russians and their Sputnik, and the first American satellite, Explorer, that went up in January. Every newsreel had a rocket in it that summer.
scenes.caption: THE NEWSREEL

scenes.text: And then the double feature. Two movies for the price of one. The first one was for the family, a Western, or a Disney picture. The second one, after ten o'clock, was for the teenagers. Monster movies. In the fall of fifty-eight there was one called The Blob, with a young actor named Steve McQueen, about a pink jelly from outer space that ate a whole town. I had nightmares for a month.
scenes.caption: THE BLOB

scenes.text: And there was Vertigo, and South Pacific, and The Defiant Ones, and a movie called Thunder Road, about moonshiners, that every boy in Ohio saw nine times. Movies were the biggest thing in the world back then. There was no other way to see a story that big.
scenes.caption: THE DOUBLE FEATURE

scenes.text: Between the two movies there was intermission. And that's when the hot dogs danced. A little cartoon came on the screen, with a hot dog and a box of popcorn and a candy bar singing, let's all go to the lobby, to get ourselves a treat. And a clock counting down, ten minutes until showtime. Every kid in that field begged for a quarter.
scenes.caption: LET'S ALL GO TO THE LOBBY

scenes.text: The snack bar was a long low building in the middle of the field with the projector booth on top. Inside it was hot and loud and smelled like grease and popcorn. A hot dog was twenty-five cents. A box of popcorn was a dime. A Coke was a dime. And they sold pizza, which in Ohio in nineteen fifty-eight was an exotic foreign food. My father thought it was Italian toast.
scenes.caption: ITALIAN TOAST

scenes.text: Now, the snack bar line was the real show. Every family in town was in it, in their pajamas and curlers and slippers. You'd see your teacher in her bathrobe buying a Mars bar. You'd see the minister's son sneaking a cigarette behind the building. It was the only place in Mansfield where nobody dressed up and nobody cared.
scenes.caption: THE TEACHER IN HER BATHROBE

scenes.text: And they sold a little green coil called PIC that you lit on the dashboard, and it burned all night with a thin smoke to keep the mosquitoes away. Ohio mosquitoes in July, sweetheart. They were the size of sparrows. That smoke would fill the car, and Mother would say, roll your window down, and the mosquitoes would come in. You couldn't win.
scenes.caption: THE GREEN COIL

scenes.text: And if it rained? Oh, sweetheart, the show went on. You turned on the windshield wipers every few minutes, swish, swish, and watched the movie through the streaks. My father kept the engine running so the defroster would work, and the whole car smelled like warm rubber and wet dog. Some of my favorite movies I only ever saw through rain.
scenes.caption: THROUGH THE RAIN

scenes.text: In the spring and fall, when Ohio nights got cold, some drive-ins rented little electric heaters that plugged in at the speaker pole. A quarter a night. You put it on the floor of the car, and it glowed orange, and it smelled like burning dust, and it kept your toes warm through the whole double feature. In November the drive-in closed for the winter, and the big screen stood there empty in the snow until April. I used to feel sorry for it.
scenes.caption: EMPTY IN THE SNOW

scenes.text: And here's something you won't believe. On Sunday mornings, some drive-ins became churches. A minister stood on top of the snack bar with a microphone, and people listened from their cars through the speakers, in their Sunday clothes. A preacher in California started a whole famous church that way in nineteen fifty-five. In Mansfield, the Lutherans tried it one summer. Grandma Pearl said it wasn't proper to pray in an Oldsmobile.
scenes.caption: CHURCH IN THE CAR

scenes.text: Now, the back row. Your mother will tell me not to say this. The back row was where the teenagers parked. And the windows of those cars fogged up so fast, honey, they couldn't have seen the movie if they'd tried. People called the drive-in the passion pit. There were ushers with flashlights who walked up and down the back row, knocking on windows.
scenes.caption: THE PASSION PIT

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty, when I was sixteen, a boy took me to the drive-in for the very first time without my parents. In his own car. My father made him come in the house and shake his hand, and told him to have me home by eleven-thirty. The movie didn't end until eleven-forty. That boy drove me home before the end. He was a gentleman. That boy was your grandfather. I married him three years later.
scenes.caption: HOME BY ELEVEN-THIRTY

scenes.text: At the end of the second movie, they played the national anthem on some screens, and a thousand engines started at once. The headlights came on, one row after another, like a field full of fireflies waking up. And the line to get out went on for half an hour. My father hummed in the dark the whole time, with Danny and me asleep under the blanket.
scenes.caption: A THOUSAND ENGINES

scenes.text: And that's the moment I remember most, sweetheart. Not the movie. The ride home. The smell of the cornfields through the window, the radio playing low, Mother's head on Father's shoulder. Feeling the car slow down and turn into our driveway, and pretending to be asleep so Father would carry me in.
scenes.caption: THE RIDE HOME

scenes.text: So what happened to the drive-ins? Well, honey, a lot of things. Daylight saving time pushed the start of the movies later and later. Color television came into every living room. The land under those big fields got too valuable, right next to the new highways, and somebody always wanted to build a mall there. The Springmill closed in the seventies. It's a parking lot now.
scenes.caption: A PARKING LOT NOW

scenes.text: There are still a few of them, scattered around the country, and some even came back for a little while during the pandemic. If you ever see one, sweetheart, you go. Bring a blanket and a bag of popcorn. Wear your pajamas. And roll your window down, even if the mosquitoes come in.
scenes.caption: IF YOU EVER SEE ONE

scenes.text: Now tell me, did your grandparents have a drive-in in their town? What was it called? What did they see there? Write it in the comments, I want to know. Come back tomorrow, sweetheart. Goodnight.
scenes.caption: GOODNIGHT, SWEETHEART
